k-1.x_notes: Strengths: five real activities with a clear progression. P1 counts greens on actual-size block outlines (2, 3, 6, 4). P2 has six actual-size hexagons for different fillings. P3 has two stars; the blue-only tiling of the 12-triangle star is forced and unique, which I checked, and the page asks whether there is more than one way. P4 covers side-2, 3 and 4 triangles with greens (4, 9, 16) and asks which upscale big green fits each. P5 is a true K-1 entry to kernel 1: blues plus as few greens as possible, minimum 2, 3, 4, then 'what do you notice?'. The boards are correctly sized, the recording boxes are usable, and the mathematics is correct throughout. Weaknesses: Name field; a title above every problem; 'Talk about it' and 'Your turn!' boxes that hold adult discussion prompts; cutesy exclamations ('Cover it all up!', 'a new way!'); a non-standard footer. P1 is quick and easy.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: clean organizer-style format (header, footer, 'Problem N:'), concise text, and actual-size outline boards with no grid lines, which makes real spatial puzzles. The chevron-only arrow and star both work (verified 2 and 3 chevrons), and the blue-only long hexagon is a genuine puzzle. Weaknesses: every task is 'fill the shape', with no counting, comparing, recording or question, and nothing reaches kernel 1 (no impossible or fewest-gap idea). 'Then fill it again with any small pieces you like' is filler with no goal. Filling the mountain with greens is trivial. Recording depends on an adult tracing. It will likely run out well before 40 minutes. This is exactly the 'too dumbed down, ends too early' complaint.
k-1.reason: X gives kindergartners and first graders more concrete work with real mathematics in it: counting, upscale blocks, a forced tiling, and the fewest-greens entry to the coloring idea. Y is clean but thin and will end early. X's format problems are boxes and text that can be deleted quickly.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: very well chosen boards, all verified. In P2 every board has even area, and two are impossible because of up/down imbalance (side-2 triangle with 3 up and 1 down; inverted trapezoid with 3 up and 5 down). P3 is the broken-hexagon pair, each with 22 white triangles: one is impossible (10 up, 12 down) and one is tileable (4 tilings). This is a true mutilated-checkerboard analogue. P4 and P5 work toward fewest greens = side length, with a table predicting sides 6 and 10. Plenty of work. Weaknesses: the thinking is given away. P1 makes children dot up-triangles and tabulate up/down coverage before they ever meet an impossible board. P2 tells them to count ups and downs. The talk boxes point at whether greens sit on up or down triangles, and P5 prints the hint 'each blue covers one up and one down' and 'try covering a purple with blues'. Also: Name field, a title on every problem, many Talk boxes, labels such as 'Purple puzzle' and 'A plan that always works?', and exclamations. It organizes before children act.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: clean format and three substantial problems that follow act, then record, then explain. P2 packs side-2 to side-5 triangles, side 5 on its own large page, and leaves 'explain why you cannot leave fewer' open, with no printed hint. P3 compares blues and purple chevrons on six actual-size boards. I verified the minimum empty spaces as A 0/0, B 0/4, C 0/0, D 0/2, E 1/1, F 2/4 (blues/purples). That shows chevrons never beat blues and sometimes do worse, which covers the last part of kernel 1 well. All mathematics is correct. Weaknesses: both impossible boards in P1 have odd area (9 and 11), so the first obstruction children meet is plain parity. The even-area impossibility only appears in P2. Children get no up/down scaffold, so the adult must lead them to the coloring argument.
grades-2-3.reason: X has the better obstruction boards, especially the broken hexagons, but it hands children the up/down invariant and the hints before they discover anything, and it is cluttered. Y covers the same kernel plus a stronger chevron comparison, keeps the explanation open, and reads like the organizer's own page, though its first problem is weaker.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a rich arc, all verified. P1 does the unit hexagon, the flip and the cube view. P2 finds all tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon (6). P3 builds the flip map and asks for the fewest flips from X (LLRR) to Y (RRLL), which is 4, the diameter, with 'how do you know'. It also asks about odd round trips. P4 introduces ribbon words, counts the tilings as C(4,2)=6, shows that a flip swaps an adjacent LR, and uses the L-score to prove that round trips have even length. P5 extends to the side-2 hexagon: two non-crossing ribbons, 20 tilings, and stacked-cube shading. The example ribbons and shading are correct, the boards are actual size, and the flip-map workspace is good. Weaknesses: Name field; titles; a cutesy 'secret code' with a 'Coming up' teaser box; a Tips box with group roles and a flip hint; a 'Challenge' label. The L-score hint gives the parity proof idea away. Problems are split into numbered sub-steps. Eight drawing boxes for six tilings is a minor issue.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: clean format and precise, clear instructions on the same 1-2-2 hexagon. The six cards are exactly the six tilings, which I verified as RRLL, RLRL, LRRL, RLLR, LRLR, LLRR. The flip example A to B is correct, and the shortest route from A to F is 4. The page leads from ribbon codes to matching the codes to tilings, rebuilding a tiling from its ribbon (both examples are uniquely determined), and the rule flip = swapping an adjacent LR. Weaknesses: P2 prints all six tilings right after P1 asks children to find as many as they can, which gives away the search and the completeness question. P5–P10 are many small, directed steps; P6 repeats the same tracing four times. The round-trip parity is never tied to the swap rule. There is no stacks-of-cubes view and no larger hexagon, so the scope is narrower for a strong fifth grader.
grades-4-5.reason: X develops more mathematics and builds it better: exhaustive search, the flip graph, ribbon counting, a parity proof, the bigger hexagon and the 3D view. Y is cleaner but gives away the tilings on page 2 and splits the work into small steps. X's clutter and teaser can be deleted in a few minutes.

overall.reason: X has correct, substantial mathematics in every band and is clearly better for K-1, where Y's fill-the-shape pages are thin and would end early. It is also somewhat richer for grades 4-5. Y is consistently cleaner, keeps the thinking open, and is slightly better for grades 2-3. X's main faults (Name fields, Talk/Tips/Coming-up boxes, cutesy wording, printed hints) can mostly be fixed by deleting text within the editing time.
